newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China, Red Cross to restart talks on prison visits.
newsitem.headline: China, Red Cross to restart talks on prison visits.

text.p: Chinese officials have told the International Committee of the Red Cross that they are ready to restart negotiations on access to thousands of political prisoners in China, an ICRC spokesman said on Monday.
Joerg Stoecklin said the negotiations, interrupted nearly three years ago, were expected to resume with a meeting of a joint expert committee in Beijing in April or May.
"We have got confirmation from Beijing through diplomatic channels that China would like to continue the technical meetings on access to political detainees," he told Reuters.
In a move signalling a change of thinking, Chinese authorities informed the ICRC in diplomatic meetings in Geneva in January of their desire to resume the negotiations.

The Geneva-based ICRC had its first official contact with Beijing on access to prisoners in January 1994. The two sides set up a technical commission of experts which met in April 1994 but a second meeting scheduled for March 1995 never took place.
Stoecklin, spokesman for Asia and the Pacific region, said there had been no discussions with the Chinese so far on the categories of prisoners the ICRC would like to visit.
The latest Chinese move could be an indication that Beijing may be moving towards a deal with Washington on human rights, one of the chief strains on relations between the two countries.

Last week, China said it was considering signing two key international human rights covenants, a move that would fulfil the first part of a U.S. plan to remove a key irritant in Sino-U.S. relations after almost eight years of tension since it crushed the 1989 Tiananmen Square pro-democracy protests.

The New York Times said on the eve of a China visit by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright that the two countries were close to an accord under which Washington would drop moves to censure Beijing at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva in exchange for a series of Chinese concessions.

It said that under the possible deal, China would sign the two international treaties in human rights, release a representative group of prisoners and resume talks with the ICRC on visits to determine the status of political prisoners.

The latest Chinese move comes just before the annual United Nations Human Rights Commission talks starting on March 10 in Geneva, where Beijing is likely to come under fire from the West for its human rights record, and ahead of an expected visit to China by U.S. Vice President Al Gore in March or April.
Stoecklin cautioned the ICRC wanted to see the humanitarian agenda on prison visits separated from the political agenda.

"For obvious reasons from past experience, the ICRC wishes to act on this issue in a very independent way," he said. "We would like to make clear to all parties that we would like to distinguish the humanitarian agenda from the political agenda."
U.S.-based Chinese human rights groups say official figures put the number of political prisoners in China at more than 3,000 but they say the true figure is probably much higher.
